question.full_text:
A very long conducting wire is bent in a semi-circular shape from $A$ to $B$ as shown in figure. The magnetic field at point $P$ for steady current configuration is given by
[Figure: Long wire with a semicircular bend from A to B, point P at the centre of the semicircle]
(1) $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}$ pointed away from the page
(2) $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$ pointed away from page
(3) $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$ pointed into the page
(4) $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}$ pointed into the page
question.html:
A very long conducting wire is bent in a semi-circular shape from A to B as shown in figure. The magnetic field at point P for steady current configuration is given by
  1. (1)μ0 i4R pointed away from the page
  2. (2)μ0 i4R[1-2π] pointed away from page
  3. (3)μ0 i4R[1-2π] pointed into the page
  4. (4)μ0 i4R pointed into the page
question.stem: A very long conducting wire is bent in a semi-circular shape from $A$ to $B$ as shown in figure. The magnetic field at point $P$ for steady current configuration is given by

figures.text: Long wire with a semicircular bend from A to B, point P at the centre of the semicircle

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Long wire with a semicircular bend from A to B, point P at the centre of the semicircle

options.text: $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}$ pointed away from the page

steps: $P$ is the centre of the semicircle, and $A$, $B$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the two semi-infinite straight wires, each at distance $R$.
Semicircular arc (current from $A$ down the left side to $B$): $B_{arc} = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}$, directed out of the page by the right-hand rule.
Upper semi-infinite wire (current rightward, $P$ below it, ending at $A$): $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$, into the page.
Lower semi-infinite wire (current leftward, $P$ above it, starting at $B$): $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4\pi R}$, into the page.
Net: $B = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4R} - \frac{2\mu_0 i}{4\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$, out of the page, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. P is the centre of the semicircle, and A, B are the feet of the perpendiculars from P to the two semi-infinite straight wires, each at distance R.
  2. Semicircular arc (current from A down the left side to B): Barc = μ0 i4R, directed out of the page by the right-hand rule.
  3. Upper semi-infinite wire (current rightward, P below it, ending at A): B1 = μ0 i4π R, into the page.
  4. Lower semi-infinite wire (current leftward, P above it, starting at B): B2 = μ0 i4π R, into the page.
  5. Net: B = μ0 i4R - 2μ0 i4π R = μ0 i4R[1-2π], out of the page, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Semicircle gives mu0 i/4R out of page; each semi-infinite straight wire gives mu0 i/(4 pi R) into page; net mu0 i/4R (1 - 2/pi) out of page.

chapter.name: Magnetic Effect of Electric Current
chapter.why: The answer is found by adding the Biot-Savart fields of the semicircular arc and the straight wire segments at P, which is the magnetic effect of electric current.

subtopics.name: Magnetic Field Due to a Current Element, Biot–Savart Law
subtopics.why: The answer comes from using the Biot–Savart law to add the field at the centre of a semicircular arc (mu0 i/4R) to the opposing fields of the two semi-infinite straight wires (mu0 i/4piR each).

step_list: Recall the field at the centre of a semicircular arc, mu0 i / 4R, and find its direction from the arc's current sense by the right-hand rule
Recognise that P lies on the perpendicular through the end of each straight wire, so each semi-infinite wire contributes mu0 i / 4piR
Find the direction of each straight wire's field at P and see that both wires point the same way, opposite to the arc's field
Combine the opposing contributions as mu0 i/4R - 2 mu0 i/4piR and assign the net direction from the larger (arc) term
difficulty.why: The work is superposing three Biot-Savart contributions (one semicircular arc and two semi-infinite wires ending in line with P), getting each direction from the right-hand rule, and subtracting the wire terms from the arc term.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The options pair each magnitude with both directions, so a candidate who ignores the straight wires (or adds rather than subtracts them) or slips on one right-hand-rule direction lands exactly on a distractor.

source.note: Stem figure (wire with semicircle A to B, radius R, point P, currents i) is in the crop; labels not transcribed here. Option 2 prints 'pointed away from page' (no 'the'), copied as printed.

categories.concept: At the centre of a semicircular arc the field is $\mu_0 i/4R$, and each semi-infinite straight wire ending on the perpendicular foot adds $\mu_0 i/4\pi R$, the straight pair opposing the arc here

trap.label: reversed
trap.route: Both contributions are found and subtracted correctly to give the magnitude $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$, and the right-hand rule is then turned the other way for the surviving term. Against the printed key the resultant is away from the page, so only the sense fails.
trap.who: a student who has done the whole calculation -- arc $\mu_0 i/4R$, two straight halves $2 \times \mu_0 i/4\pi R$ -- and then takes the sense from the term that was subtracted
trap.feels: the magnitude matches the key exactly, so the answer looks fully worked, and the arc and the straight pair carry opposite senses, so whichever is written last reads as the resultant's direction

steps.text: Arc at its centre: $\mu_0 i/4R$. Each semi-infinite straight wire with its end at the foot of the perpendicular: $\mu_0 i/4\pi R$.
The straight pair opposes the arc, so the magnitudes subtract: $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$.
Give the resultant the sense of the term that was taken away.
steps.fix: The resultant keeps the sense of the LARGER term; curl the right hand once for the dominant contribution and let the smaller one only shrink it.

other_options.who: a student who sees the semicircle, writes down the half-ring result $\mu_0 i/4R$, and treats the long straight portions as contributing nothing at $P$
other_options.feels: the straight wires look like the standard case of a point on a wire's own line, where the contribution vanishes, and $\mu_0 i/4R$ is the memorised half-ring value

steps.text: The semicircular bend contributes $\mu_0 i/4R$ at its centre $P$.
The straight parts give nothing at $P$, so that is the whole field.
steps.fix: $P$ is not on either straight wire's line: each lies a perpendicular distance $R$ away and ends on that perpendicular, so each adds $\mu_0 i/4\pi R$ -- which is where the $2/\pi$ in the answer comes from.

other_options.proof: The four options are a two-by-two grid: the arc-only magnitude $\mu_0 i/4R$ or the full $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}[1-\frac{2}{\pi}]$, crossed with the two senses. Option 4 is the only corner needing two independent mistakes at once -- the straight wires dropped AND the right-hand rule inverted -- whereas each other corner is one step from the correct working. No single step of the Biot-Savart sum produces it.

categories.reason: This question requires the arc's field and the two semi-infinite straight fields summed with their senses, demonstrated by each option pairing a magnitude with a direction -- "$\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}\left[1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right]$ pointed into the page" -- so both parts must hold at once.
categories.note: The E1 pattern called this statement_options from a count of sentence-shaped options; the printed shape is a magnitude plus a direction that must both be right, which is two_part. Tagged as printed. Working the figure exactly as transcribed in this packet -- current in along the lower wire, round the left of the arc, out along the upper wire -- puts the arc's contribution into the page and the straight pair's out of it, making the resultant into the page, i.e. option 3, while the printed key is option 2; the magnitude $\frac{\mu_0 i}{4R}[1-\frac{2}{\pi}]$ is the same either way. A reviewer holding the printed figure should check the arrow senses on the two straight portions: if they are as transcribed, the trap and option 1 exchange directions and the labels stay as they are.
categories.flag_why: The current senses as transcribed give the opposite direction to the printed key; the magnitude agrees with the key.

question.full_text:
The resistance of platinum wire at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is $2\,\Omega$ and $6.8\,\Omega$ at $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the wire is
(1) $3 \times 10^{-3}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$
(2) $3 \times 10^{-2}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$
(3) $3 \times 10^{-1}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$
(4) $3 \times 10^{-4}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$
question.html:
The resistance of platinum wire at 0°C is 2 Ω and 6.8 Ω at 80°C. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the wire is
  1. (1)3 × 10-3 °C-1
  2. (2)3 × 10-2 °C-1
  3. (3)3 × 10-1 °C-1
  4. (4)3 × 10-4 °C-1
question.stem: The resistance of platinum wire at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is $2\,\Omega$ and $6.8\,\Omega$ at $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the wire is

steps: Use $R_T = R_0(1 + \alpha T)$, so $\alpha = \frac{R_T - R_0}{R_0 T}$.
$R_T - R_0 = 6.8\,\Omega - 2\,\Omega = 4.8\,\Omega$.
$R_0 T = 2\,\Omega \times 80^{\circ}\mathrm{C} = 160\,\Omega\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
$\alpha = \frac{4.8}{160} = 0.03 = 3 \times 10^{-2}\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}^{-1}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Use RT = R0(1 + α T), so α = RT - R0R0 T.
  2. RT - R0 = 6.8 Ω - 2 Ω = 4.8 Ω.
  3. R0 T = 2 Ω × 80°C = 160 Ω °C.
  4. α = 4.8160 = 0.03 = 3 × 10-2 °C-1, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: R_T = R_0(1 + alpha T), so alpha = (6.8 - 2)/(2 x 80) = 4.8/160 = 3 x 10^-2 per degree C.

chapter.name: Current Electricity
chapter.why: The answer depends on the temperature dependence of resistance, R = R0(1 + alpha*T), giving alpha = (6.8-2)/(2*80) = 3 x 10^-2 per degree C, which is taught in Current Electricity.

subtopics.name: Temperature Coefficient of Resistance
subtopics.why: The answer comes from R_t = R_0(1 + alpha t), giving alpha = (6.8 - 2)/(2 x 80) = 3 x 10^-2 per degree C, which is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

step_list: Substitute R0 = 2 ohm, R = 6.8 ohm and delta T = 80 C into R = R0(1 + alpha delta T) and solve for alpha = (R - R0)/(R0 delta T)
difficulty.why: A single substitution into the NCERT linear temperature-dependence formula for resistance, with simple arithmetic.

categories.concept: The temperature coefficient is the fractional change of resistance per degree referred to the resistance at $0^{\circ}$C: $\alpha = (R - R_0)/(R_0\,\Delta t)$

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: $\alpha = 4.8/(2 \times 80)$ is set up correctly and the division is finished one decimal place out, giving $0.003$ instead of $0.03$. All four options print the same mantissa 3, so the whole question rests on where that decimal lands: $4.8/160 = 0.03 = 3 \times 10^{-2}$.

[Figure: Thin biconvex lens of index n1 = 1.5 embedded in a medium of index n2 = 1.6]

question.stem: In the figure shown here, what is the equivalent focal length of the combination of lenses (Assume that all layers are thin)?

figures.text: Thin biconvex lens of index n1 = 1.5 embedded in a medium of index n2 = 1.6

checks.print_match: not a vector figure: drawn from the spec

spec.title: Thin biconvex lens of index n1 = 1.5 embedded in a medium of index n2 = 1.6

steps: The slab of $n_2 = 1.6$ with the lens of $n_1 = 1.5$ inside acts as three thin lenses in contact in air: plano-concave ($n_2$), biconvex ($n_1$), plano-concave ($n_2$).
Biconvex lens: $\frac{1}{f_1} = (1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{20}\right) = \frac{1}{20}\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.
Each plano-concave lens: $\frac{1}{f_2} = (1.6-1)\left(\frac{1}{\infty}-\frac{1}{20}\right) = -\frac{3}{100}\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.
Lenses in contact: $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{20} - 2\times\frac{3}{100} = \frac{5}{100}-\frac{6}{100} = -\frac{1}{100}\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.
$F = -100\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The slab of n2 = 1.6 with the lens of n1 = 1.5 inside acts as three thin lenses in contact in air: plano-concave (n2), biconvex (n1), plano-concave (n2).
  2. Biconvex lens: 1f1 = (1.5-1)(120+120) = 120 cm-1.
  3. Each plano-concave lens: 1f2 = (1.6-1)(1∞-120) = -3100 cm-1.
  4. Lenses in contact: 1F = 120 - 2×3100 = 5100-6100 = -1100 cm-1.
  5. F = -100 cm, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: In air the system is a biconvex n=1.5 lens (P=+1/20) between two plano-concave n=1.6 lenses (each P=-0.6/20=-3/100); net P=-1/100, so f=-100 cm.

question.stem: A wire carrying a current $I$ along the positive $x$-axis has length $L$. It is kept in a magnetic field $\vec{B} = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k})\,\mathrm{T}$. The magnitude of the magnetic force acting on the wire is

steps: The force on a straight current-carrying wire is $\vec{F} = I\vec{L} \times \vec{B}$ with $\vec{L} = L\hat{i}$.
$\hat{i} \times (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}) = 0 + 3\hat{k} + 4\hat{j}$, so $\vec{F} = IL(4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})$.
$|\vec{F}| = IL\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\,IL$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The force on a straight current-carrying wire is →F = I→L × →B with →L = Lˆı.
  2. ˆı × (2ˆı + 3ˆȷ - 4ˆk) = 0 + 3ˆk + 4ˆȷ, so →F = IL(4ˆȷ + 3ˆk).
  3. |→F| = IL42 + 32 = 5 IL, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: F = IL(i x B) = IL(3k + 4j), magnitude sqrt(9+16) IL = 5IL.

steps: Heterogeneous catalysis means the catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants.
Option 1: sugar solution and $\mathrm{H^{+}}$ ions are both in the aqueous phase, so homogeneous.
Option 2: $\mathrm{O_3(g)}$ with $\mathrm{NO(g)}$ are both gases, so homogeneous.
Option 4: $\mathrm{2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \xrightarrow{NO(g)} 2SO_3(g)}$ is all gas phase, so homogeneous (lead chamber process).
Option 3: $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \xrightarrow{Fe(s)} 2NH_3(g)}$ has a solid catalyst with gaseous reactants, so heterogeneous, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Heterogeneous catalysis means the catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants.
  2. Option 1: sugar solution and H+ ions are both in the aqueous phase, so homogeneous.
  3. Option 2: O3(g) with NO(g) are both gases, so homogeneous.
  4. Option 4: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) NO(g)  2SO3(g) is all gas phase, so homogeneous (lead chamber process).
  5. Option 3: N2(g) + 3H2(g) Fe(s)  2NH3(g) has a solid catalyst with gaseous reactants, so heterogeneous, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Haber process: gaseous N2 and H2 react on solid finely divided Fe catalyst, so catalyst and reactants are in different phases (heterogeneous); the other three are single-phase (homogeneous).

steps: Boyle's law at constant $n$ and $T$: $PV = nRT$, so $P = nRT\cdot\frac{1}{V}$.
A plot of $P$ against $\frac{1}{V}$ is a straight line through the origin with slope $nRT$.
Higher $T$ gives a larger slope, so with $T_3 > T_2 > T_1$ the $T_3$ line is steepest; option $1$ shows exactly this.
Option $2$ draws $P$ vs $\frac{1}{V}$ as hyperbolas, which is wrong.
Option $3$ is $P$ vs $T$ at constant $V$ (Gay-Lussac's law), not Boyle's law.
Option $4$ is $P$ vs $V$ hyperbolas, but the outermost curve is labelled $T_1$ although $T_3 > T_2 > T_1$; the outermost isotherm should be $T_3$, so the labelling is wrong.
Only option $1$ is a correct Boyle's law graph.
ai_solution.html:
1. Boyle's law at constant n and T: PV = nRT, so P = nRT·1V.
  2. A plot of P against 1V is a straight line through the origin with slope nRT.
  3. Higher T gives a larger slope, so with T3 > T2 > T1 the T3 line is steepest; option 1 shows exactly this.
  4. Option 2 draws P vs 1V as hyperbolas, which is wrong.
  5. Option 3 is P vs T at constant V (Gay-Lussac's law), not Boyle's law.
  6. Option 4 is P vs V hyperbolas, but the outermost curve is labelled T1 although T3 > T2 > T1; the outermost isotherm should be T3, so the labelling is wrong.
  7. Only option 1 is a correct Boyle's law graph.
ai_solution.why: Boyle's law PV = nRT gives P proportional to 1/V: straight lines through origin with slope nRT, so the highest temperature T3 has the steepest line, as in option 1.

question.full_text:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R : In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
(Assertion A) A reaction can have zero activation energy.
(Reasons R) The minimum extra amount of energy absorbed by reactant molecules so that their energy becomes equal to threshold value, is called activation energy.
(1) Both A and R are true and R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(2) A is true but R is false
(3) A is false but R is true
(4) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

steps: Activation energy is $E_a = E_{threshold} - E_{reactants}$; if reactant molecules already possess the threshold energy, $E_a = 0$, so A is true.
R states the standard definition of activation energy as the extra energy needed to reach the threshold value, so R is true.
The definition in R does not account for why $E_a$ can be zero, so R is not the correct explanation of A, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Activation energy is Ea = Ethreshold - Ereactants; if reactant molecules already possess the threshold energy, Ea = 0, so A is true.
  2. R states the standard definition of activation energy as the extra energy needed to reach the threshold value, so R is true.
  3. The definition in R does not account for why Ea can be zero, so R is not the correct explanation of A, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: A is true (Ea = threshold energy - average energy of reactants can be zero, e.g. radical recombination); R correctly defines activation energy but does not explain why it can be zero.

steps: Protonation of the $-OH$ by $\mathrm{HBr}$ gives $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH(OH_2^+)CH_3}$.
Loss of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ gives the secondary carbocation $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3}$.
A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 gives the more stable tertiary carbocation $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\overset{+}{C}-CH_2-CH_3}$.
Attack of $\mathrm{Br^-}$ gives $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(Br)-CH_2-CH_3}$ (2-bromo-2-methylbutane), which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Protonation of the -OH by HBr gives (CH3)2CH-CH(OH2+)CH3.
  2. Loss of H2O gives the secondary carbocation (CH3)2CH-+CH-CH3.

steps: Initial rate: $r = k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}]$.
With $[\mathrm{A}]$ tripled and $[\mathrm{B}]$ constant: $r' = k(3[\mathrm{A}])^2[\mathrm{B}]$.
$r' = 9k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}] = 9r$, so the rate increases by a factor of nine, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Initial rate: r = k[A]2[B].
  2. With [A] tripled and [B] constant: r' = k(3[A])2[B].
  3. r' = 9k[A]2[B] = 9r, so the rate increases by a factor of nine, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Rate is second order in A, so tripling [A] multiplies the rate by 3^2 = 9.

  4. Graphite's layers slide over each other, so it is used as a dry lubricant: D → II.

ai_solution.why: Coke is a reducing agent (III), diamond has sp3 carbon (I), fullerene is cage-like (IV), graphite is a dry lubricant (II).

A compound is formed by two elements A and B. The element B forms cubic close packed structure and atoms of A occupy $1/3$ of tetrahedral voids. If the formula of the compound is $\mathrm{A_xB_y}$, then the value of $x + y$ is in option

(2) $3$
(3) $2$
(4) $5$
question.html:

question.stem: A compound is formed by two elements A and B. The element B forms cubic close packed structure and atoms of A occupy $1/3$ of tetrahedral voids. If the formula of the compound is $\mathrm{A_xB_y}$, then the value of $x + y$ is in option

steps: Let the number of B atoms in the ccp lattice be $N$.
A ccp lattice has $2N$ tetrahedral voids.
A occupies $\frac{1}{3}$ of them: $n_A = \frac{1}{3}(2N) = \frac{2N}{3}$.
$A : B = \frac{2N}{3} : N = 2 : 3$, so the formula is $\mathrm{A_2B_3}$.
$x + y = 2 + 3 = 5$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Let the number of B atoms in the ccp lattice be N.
  2. A ccp lattice has 2N tetrahedral voids.
  3. A occupies 13 of them: nA = 13(2N) = 2N3.
  4. A : B = 2N3 : N = 2 : 3, so the formula is A2B3.
  5. x + y = 2 + 3 = 5, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: ccp of B gives 2N tetrahedral voids per N atoms of B; A fills 1/3, so A:B = 2N/3 : N = 2:3, formula A2B3, x + y = 5.

ai_solution.html:
1. A homoleptic complex has the metal bound to only one kind of ligand.
  2. Option 1 is [Pt(NH3)2Cl(NO2)] with NH3, Cl- and NO2-: heteroleptic.
  3. Option 2 is [Co(NH3)5(CO3)]Cl with NH3 and CO32-: heteroleptic.
  4. Option 3 is [Cr(NH3)3(H2O)3]Cl3 with NH3 and H2O: heteroleptic.
  5. Option 4 is K3[Al(C2O4)3] with only C2O42- ligands: homoleptic, so the answer is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Only potassium trioxalatoaluminate(III), K3[Al(C2O4)3], has a single kind of ligand (oxalate) bound to the metal; the others have mixed ligands.

question.stem: The correct order of energies of molecular orbitals of $\mathrm{N_2}$ molecule, is

steps: For molecules up to $\mathrm{N_2}$ (total electrons $\le 14$), $2s$-$2p$ mixing raises the energy of $\sigma 2p_z$ above the degenerate $\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y$ pair.
So the order is $\sigma 1s < \sigma^{*}1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^{*}2s < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi^{*}2p_x = \pi^{*}2p_y) < \sigma^{*}2p_z$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For molecules up to N2 (total electrons ≤ 14), 2s-2p mixing raises the energy of σ 2pz above the degenerate π 2px = π 2py pair.
  2. So the order is σ 1s < σ*1s < σ 2s < σ*2s < (π 2px = π 2py) < σ 2pz < (π*2px = π*2py) < σ*2pz, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: For N2 (up to 14 electrons) s-p mixing raises sigma2pz above the degenerate pi2p pair, giving pi2p < sigma2pz < pi*2p < sigma*2pz.

question.full_text:
Taking stability as the factor, which one of the following represents correct relationship?
(1) $\mathrm{InI_3} > \mathrm{InI}$
(2) $\mathrm{AlCl} > \mathrm{AlCl_3}$
(3) $\mathrm{TlI} > \mathrm{TlI_3}$
(4) $\mathrm{TlCl_3} > \mathrm{TlCl}$
question.html:
Taking stability as the factor, which one of the following represents correct relationship?
  1. (1)InI3 > InI
  2. (2)AlCl > AlCl3
  3. (3)TlI > TlI3
  4. (4)TlCl3 > TlCl
question.stem: Taking stability as the factor, which one of the following represents correct relationship?

steps: Down group 13 the inert pair effect makes the $+1$ oxidation state increasingly stable relative to $+3$.
For Al, $+3$ is the stable state, so $\mathrm{AlCl_3} > \mathrm{AlCl}$; option $2$ is wrong.
For Tl, $+1$ is more stable than $+3$, so $\mathrm{TlCl} > \mathrm{TlCl_3}$ (option $4$ wrong) and $\mathrm{TlI} > \mathrm{TlI_3}$, which is option $3$.
Option $1$ ($\mathrm{InI_3} > \mathrm{InI}$) is not the intended relationship; the clear inert-pair case is Tl, so the answer is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Down group 13 the inert pair effect makes the +1 oxidation state increasingly stable relative to +3.
  2. For Al, +3 is the stable state, so AlCl3 > AlCl; option 2 is wrong.
  3. For Tl, +1 is more stable than +3, so TlCl > TlCl3 (option 4 wrong) and TlI > TlI3, which is option 3.
  4. Option 1 (InI3 > InI) is not the intended relationship; the clear inert-pair case is Tl, so the answer is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Inert pair effect: down group 13 the +1 state becomes more stable than +3, so for Tl the +1 compound TlI is more stable than TlI3; Al prefers +3 and In +3 is still favoured over +1.

steps: A is false: atoms are made of three fundamental particles (electron, proton, neutron), not two.
B is true: $m_e = 9.10939 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
C is true: isotopes have the same atomic number and electronic configuration, so they show the same chemical properties.
D is false: nucleons are protons and neutrons, not protons and electrons.
E is true: Dalton's atomic theory regarded the atom as the ultimate, indivisible particle of matter.
The correct statements are B, C and E, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A is false: atoms are made of three fundamental particles (electron, proton, neutron), not two.
  2. B is true: me = 9.10939 × 10-31 kg.
  3. C is true: isotopes have the same atomic number and electronic configuration, so they show the same chemical properties.
  4. D is false: nucleons are protons and neutrons, not protons and electrons.
  5. E is true: Dalton's atomic theory regarded the atom as the ultimate, indivisible particle of matter.
  6. The correct statements are B, C and E, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: A false (atoms have three fundamental particles), D false (nucleons are protons and neutrons); B, C and E are true.

steps: Conductivity $\kappa = \frac{G^*}{R}$, so cell constant $G^* = \kappa R$.
$G^* = 0.210\,\Omega^{-1}\mathrm{cm^{-1}} \times 60\,\Omega = 12.6\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.
No option equals $12.6\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; the digits match $1.26\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, which corresponds to $\kappa = 0.0210\,\Omega^{-1}\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so option $2$.

  2. G* = 0.210 Ω-1cm-1 × 60 Ω = 12.6 cm-1.
  3. No option equals 12.6 cm-1; the digits match 1.26 cm-1, which corresponds to κ = 0.0210 Ω-1cm-1, so option 2.
ai_solution.why: Cell constant G* = kappa x R = 0.210 x 60 = 12.6 cm^-1; no option matches, closest digits are 1.26 cm^-1 (option 2), implying kappa was meant to be 0.0210.

steps: A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor.
In $\mathrm{BF_3}$, boron has only $6$ valence electrons (incomplete octet), so it can accept a lone pair: Lewis acid.
$\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{OH^-}$ and $\mathrm{NH_3}$ all carry lone pairs and donate them: Lewis bases.
Hence the answer is $\mathrm{BF_3}$, option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor.
  2. In BF3, boron has only 6 valence electrons (incomplete octet), so it can accept a lone pair: Lewis acid.
  3. H2O, OH- and NH3 all carry lone pairs and donate them: Lewis bases.
  4. Hence the answer is BF3, option 2.
ai_solution.why: BF3 is electron-deficient (B has only 6 valence electrons) and accepts an electron pair, so it is a Lewis acid; H2O, OH- and NH3 have lone pairs and act as Lewis bases.

(1) $l = 2n_m + 1$
(2) $n_m = 2l^2 + 1$
(3) $n_m = l + 2$
(4) $l = \frac{n_m - 1}{2}$

  3. (3)nm = l + 2

question.stem: The relation between $n_m$, ($n_m$ = the number of permissible values of magnetic quantum number ($m$)) for a given value of azimuthal quantum number ($l$), is

steps: For a given $l$, $m$ takes the values $-l, \ldots, 0, \ldots, +l$.
Rearranging, $l = \frac{n_m - 1}{2}$, which is option $4$.

  2. So nm = 2l + 1.
  3. Rearranging, l = nm - 12, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: For a given l, m takes 2l+1 values, so n_m = 2l+1, i.e. l = (n_m - 1)/2.

question.full_text:
Amongst the following the total number of species NOT having eight electrons around central atom in its outer most shell, is $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ :
(1) 2
(2) 4
(3) 1
(4) 3
question.html:
Amongst the following the total number of species NOT having eight electrons around central atom in its outer most shell, is NH3, AlCl3, BeCl2, CCl4, PCl5 :
  1. (1)2
  2. (2)4
  3. (3)1
  4. (4)3
question.stem: Amongst the following the total number of species NOT having eight electrons around central atom in its outer most shell, is $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ :

steps: $\mathrm{NH_3}$: N has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair $= 8$ electrons (octet).
$\mathrm{AlCl_3}$: Al has 3 bond pairs $= 6$ electrons (incomplete octet).
$\mathrm{BeCl_2}$: Be has 2 bond pairs $= 4$ electrons (incomplete octet).
$\mathrm{CCl_4}$: C has 4 bond pairs $= 8$ electrons (octet).
$\mathrm{PCl_5}$: P has 5 bond pairs $= 10$ electrons (expanded octet).
Species not having 8 electrons: $\mathrm{AlCl_3}, \mathrm{BeCl_2}, \mathrm{PCl_5}$ $= 3$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. NH3: N has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 8 electrons (octet).
  2. AlCl3: Al has 3 bond pairs = 6 electrons (incomplete octet).
  3. BeCl2: Be has 2 bond pairs = 4 electrons (incomplete octet).
  4. CCl4: C has 4 bond pairs = 8 electrons (octet).
  5. PCl5: P has 5 bond pairs = 10 electrons (expanded octet).
  6. Species not having 8 electrons: AlCl3, BeCl2, PCl5 = 3, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: AlCl3 (6 electrons), BeCl2 (4 electrons) and PCl5 (10 electrons) lack an octet on the central atom; NH3 and CCl4 have 8, so the count is 3.

chapter.name: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
chapter.why: The answer turns on which species violate the octet rule (incomplete octet in AlCl3 and BeCl2, expanded octet in PCl5), which is taught under the Octet Rule in Chemical Bonding.

subtopics.name: Octet Rule
subtopics.why: The answer depends on identifying exceptions to the octet rule (incomplete octet in AlCl3 and BeCl2, expanded octet in PCl5), giving 3 species.

step_list: For each of the five species, count the electrons around the central atom from its valence electrons and bonds (N in NH3 with three bond pairs and one lone pair, Al in AlCl3 with three bond pairs, Be in BeCl2 with two bond pairs, C in CCl4 with four bond pairs, P in PCl5 with five bond pairs)
Classify each as octet, incomplete octet or expanded octet (recall of the NCERT octet-rule exceptions)
Apply the NOT in the stem and count the species whose total differs from eight, covering both the incomplete-octet and the expanded-octet cases
difficulty.why: The work is an electron count around the central atom for five molecules, a sort into octet, incomplete octet and expanded octet, and a count of the ones that are not eight; this is direct recall of the NCERT octet-rule exceptions applied five times.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Small traps: a candidate who thinks only of electron-deficient species may leave out the expanded octet of PCl5, and one who treats AlCl3 as its dimer Al2Cl6 may count it as having an octet. Each slip changes the count by one, which lands on a neighbouring option.

source.note: Options are plain integers; no figure. Species list printed on its own line after the stem.

categories.concept: The octet rule is broken in two directions: aluminium and beryllium halides leave the central atom short of eight electrons, while $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ puts ten around phosphorus

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: The octet test is applied in one direction only -- which central atoms are short of eight -- so $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ are counted and the expanded octet of $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ is passed over, giving 2
trap.who: a student who has learnt the octet rule through the incomplete-octet examples of boron, aluminium and beryllium
trap.feels: $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ is a familiar, perfectly ordinary covalent chloride with nothing missing from it, so it reads as a species that obeys

steps.text: $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ leaves aluminium with six electrons and $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ leaves beryllium with four, so both break the rule.
$\mathrm{NH_3}$ has three bonds and a lone pair, and $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ four bonds, so both reach eight.
That leaves two species not having eight electrons.
steps.fix: Count $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ too: five bonds put ten electrons around phosphorus, which is not eight either, so the tally is 3.

other_options.who: a student who counts only bonding pairs around the central atom and leaves lone pairs out of the total
other_options.feels: ammonia has three bonds, and three pairs is six electrons, so it looks as short of eight as $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ is

steps.text: $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ all fail the octet test.
$\mathrm{NH_3}$ has only three bonds, so add it and the tally is 4.
steps.fix: The lone pair counts towards the shell: three bonding pairs plus one lone pair is eight electrons on nitrogen.

other_options.proof: Worked the electron count for all five species: $\mathrm{NH_3}$ 8, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ 6, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ 4, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ 8, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ 10. A tally of 1 needs two of the three failures to be read as obeying, and $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ are the chapter's own printed incomplete-octet examples while $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ is its printed expanded-octet example. The smallest tally any single omission produces is 2.

categories.reason: This question requires the octet rule applied to five printed species, demonstrated by the stem listing $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ and $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ and asking for "the total number of species NOT having eight electrons around central atom".
categories.note: Vocabulary gap recorded rather than forced: what the answer WANTS here is a tally, and no asks value says that. apply_rule is used because the work is the octet criterion applied to five new cases, but its definition adds "with no quantity produced", which a count of 3 breaks; calculate does not fit either, since nothing is computed from the stem's numbers. The value this axis is missing is count_qualifying_items, which the codebook's E2 axis already carries for exactly this reason, and q094 of this same paper (how many species obey Huckel's rule) is a second instance.

answer.publisher_text: A is true but R is false

steps: $\mathrm{Na + (x+y)NH_3 \rightarrow [Na(NH_3)_x]^+ + [e(NH_3)_y]^-}$; the ammoniated electron gives the deep blue colour and makes the solution paramagnetic, so A is true.

The blue colour is due to ammoniated electrons, not amide; amide ($\mathrm{NaNH_2}$) forms only on standing ($\mathrm{Na^+ + e^- + NH_3 \rightarrow NaNH_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}H_2}$) and the blue colour is lost, so R is false: option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Na + (x+y)NH3 → [Na(NH3)x]+ + [e(NH3)y]-; the ammoniated electron gives the deep blue colour and makes the solution paramagnetic, so A is true.
  2. The blue colour is due to ammoniated electrons, not amide; amide (NaNH2) forms only on standing (Na+ + e- + NH3 → NaNH2 + 12H2) and the blue colour is lost, so R is false: option 2.
ai_solution.why: Na in liquid NH3 gives a deep blue paramagnetic solution due to ammoniated electrons, not amide (amide forms only on standing, and the solution then turns bronze/colourless), so A is true and R is false.

question.full_text:
The element expected to form largest ion to achieve the nearest noble gas configuration is
(1) $\mathrm{F}$
(2) $\mathrm{N}$
(3) $\mathrm{Na}$
(4) $\mathrm{O}$
question.html:
The element expected to form largest ion to achieve the nearest noble gas configuration is
  1. (1)F
  2. (2)N
  3. (3)Na
  4. (4)O
question.stem: The element expected to form largest ion to achieve the nearest noble gas configuration is

steps: To reach the nearest noble gas configuration (Ne) the elements form $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$, $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{F^{-}}$ and $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$, which all have $10$ electrons.
For isoelectronic ions, radius falls as nuclear charge rises: $Z = 7 < 8 < 9 < 11$.
So $\mathrm{N^{3-}} > \mathrm{O^{2-}} > \mathrm{F^{-}} > \mathrm{Na^{+}}$; the largest ion comes from $\mathrm{N}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. To reach the nearest noble gas configuration (Ne) the elements form N3-, O2-, F- and Na+, which all have 10 electrons.
  2. For isoelectronic ions, radius falls as nuclear charge rises: Z = 7 < 8 < 9 < 11.
  3. So N3- > O2- > F- > Na+; the largest ion comes from N, which is option 2.

steps: $\Delta_r G = -nFE_{\mathrm{cell}}$, where $n$ is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the reaction as written, so $\Delta_r G$ changes with $n$: A is true.
$E_{\mathrm{cell}}$ does not depend on the amount of reactants (intensive), while $\Delta_r G$ scales with the amount of reaction (extensive): R is true.
Because $E_{\mathrm{cell}}$ is fixed but $\Delta_r G$ must scale with amount, the factor $n$ carries that dependence, so R correctly explains A, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Δr G = -nFEcell, where n is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the reaction as written, so Δr G changes with n: A is true.
  2. Ecell does not depend on the amount of reactants (intensive), while Δr G scales with the amount of reaction (extensive): R is true.
  3. Because Ecell is fixed but Δr G must scale with amount, the factor n carries that dependence, so R correctly explains A, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: E_cell is intensive and Delta_rG is extensive, so Delta_rG = -nFE_cell scales with n (moles of electrons); R explains why A holds.

(4) $16$

question.stem: Weight (g) of two moles of the organic compound, which is obtained by heating sodium ethanoate with sodium hydroxide in presence of calcium oxide is :

steps: Heating sodium ethanoate with NaOH and CaO (soda lime) is decarboxylation: $\mathrm{CH_3COONa + NaOH \xrightarrow{CaO,\,\Delta} CH_4 + Na_2CO_3}$.
Molar mass of $\mathrm{CH_4} = 12 + 4(1) = 16\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
Mass of 2 mol $= 2 \times 16 = 32\,\mathrm{g}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Heating sodium ethanoate with NaOH and CaO (soda lime) is decarboxylation: CH3COONa + NaOH CaO, Δ  CH4 + Na2CO3.
  2. Molar mass of CH4 = 12 + 4(1) = 16 g mol-1.
  3. Mass of 2 mol = 2 × 16 = 32 g, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Soda-lime decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate gives methane (M = 16 g/mol); 2 mol weigh 32 g.

steps: Option 1: $\mathrm{CH_3C{\equiv}N \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2NH_2}$, a primary amine.
Option 2: $\mathrm{CH_3N{\equiv}C \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3NHCH_3}$, a secondary amine.
Option 3: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 \xrightarrow{LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2NH_2}$, a primary amine.
Option 4: Hofmann bromamide degradation, $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 \xrightarrow{Br_2/KOH} CH_3NH_2}$, a primary amine.
Only option $2$ does not give a primary amine.

1. Option 1: CH3C≡N LiAlH4  CH3CH2NH2, a primary amine.
  2. Option 2: CH3N≡C LiAlH4  CH3NHCH3, a secondary amine.
  3. Option 3: CH3CONH2 LiAlH4  CH3CH2NH2, a primary amine.
  4. Option 4: Hofmann bromamide degradation, CH3CONH2 Br2/KOH  CH3NH2, a primary amine.
  5. Only option 2 does not give a primary amine.

question.stem: The right option for the mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ produced by heating $20\,\mathrm{g}$ of $20\%$ pure limestone is (Atomic mass of Ca = $40$) $\left[\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{1200\,\mathrm{K}} \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\right]$

steps: Mass of pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 0.20 \times 20\,\mathrm{g} = 4\,\mathrm{g}$.
Molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
$n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = \frac{4}{100} = 0.04\,\mathrm{mol}$.
From $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$ (1:1), $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 0.04\,\mathrm{mol}$.
$m(\mathrm{CO_2}) = 0.04 \times 44 = 1.76\,\mathrm{g}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Mass of pure CaCO3 = 0.20 × 20 g = 4 g.
  2. Molar mass of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100 g mol-1.
  3. n(CaCO3) = 4100 = 0.04 mol.
  4. From CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (1:1), n(CO2) = 0.04 mol.
  5. m(CO2) = 0.04 × 44 = 1.76 g, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Pure CaCO3 = 20% of 20 g = 4 g = 0.04 mol, giving 0.04 mol CO2 = 0.04 x 44 = 1.76 g.

(1) 12, 3, 0

question.stem: The number of $\sigma$ bonds, $\pi$ bonds and lone pair of electrons in pyridine, respectively are:

steps: Pyridine is $\mathrm{C_5H_5N}$: a six-membered aromatic ring with one N and five C–H units.
Ring $\sigma$ bonds: $6$; C–H $\sigma$ bonds: $5$; total $\sigma = 6 + 5 = 11$.
The aromatic ring has $3$ alternating double bonds, so $\pi = 3$.
The $sp^2$ N carries $1$ lone pair (in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic sextet).
ai_solution.html:
1. Pyridine is C5H5N: a six-membered aromatic ring with one N and five C–H units.
  2. Ring σ bonds: 6; C–H σ bonds: 5; total σ = 6 + 5 = 11.
  3. The aromatic ring has 3 alternating double bonds, so π = 3.
  4. The sp2 N carries 1 lone pair (in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic sextet).
  5. (11, 3, 1) is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Pyridine C5H5N has 6 ring sigma bonds + 5 C-H sigma bonds = 11 sigma, 3 pi bonds in the aromatic ring, and 1 lone pair on N.

question.full_text:
Which amongst the following options is the correct relation between change in enthalpy and change in internal energy?
(1) $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{g}RT$
(2) $\Delta H - \Delta U = -\Delta nRT$
(3) $\Delta H + \Delta U = \Delta nR$
(4) $\Delta H = \Delta U - \Delta n_{g}RT$
question.html:
Which amongst the following options is the correct relation between change in enthalpy and change in internal energy?
  1. (1)Δ H = Δ U + Δ ngRT
  2. (2)Δ H - Δ U = -Δ nRT
  3. (3)Δ H + Δ U = Δ nR
  4. (4)Δ H = Δ U - Δ ngRT
question.stem: Which amongst the following options is the correct relation between change in enthalpy and change in internal energy?

steps: By definition $H = U + PV$, so $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta (PV)$.
For gases at constant $T$, $PV = nRT$ gives $\Delta (PV) = \Delta n_{g} RT$.
Hence $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{g} RT$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By definition H = U + PV, so Δ H = Δ U + Δ (PV).
  2. For gases at constant T, PV = nRT gives Δ (PV) = Δ ng RT.
  3. Hence Δ H = Δ U + Δ ng RT, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: From H = U + PV, for an ideal-gas reaction at constant T, Delta(PV) = Delta n_g RT, so Delta H = Delta U + Delta n_g RT.

steps.text: $\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT$ is a true form of the relation.
So, swapping the two, $\Delta H = \Delta U - \Delta n_g RT$.
steps.fix: Moving a term across the equals sign changes its sign: from $\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT$ it follows that $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$.

other_options.who: a student who writes the relation as a difference of the two state functions and then has to settle the sign of the right-hand side
other_options.feels: it is the only option written as a difference, which is how the relation is derived, so its shape looks like the derivation

steps.text: The derivation puts $\Delta H - \Delta U$ on one side and the work term on the other.
Write that work term as $-\Delta nRT$.
steps.fix: $pV = nRT$ is positive, so $\Delta H - \Delta U = +\Delta n_g RT$; the minus sign belongs only when $\Delta U - \Delta H$ is written on the left.

other_options.proof: Checked it dimensionally and against the derivation. Its right-hand side, $\Delta nR$, carries units of energy per kelvin because the temperature has been dropped, so the two sides cannot be equal whatever the signs are. It also adds the two state functions where $H = U + pV$ can only produce their difference, so no rearrangement of the definition reaches it.

question.full_text:
Which of the following statements are INCORRECT? Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
(A) All the transition metals except scandium form $\mathrm{MO}$ oxides which are ionic.
(B) The highest oxidation number corresponding to the group number in transition metal oxides is attained in $\mathrm{Sc_2O_3}$ to $\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}$.
(C) Basic character increases from $\mathrm{V_2O_3}$ to $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ to $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$.
(D) $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ dissolves in acids to give $\mathrm{VO_4^{3-}}$ salts.
(E) $\mathrm{CrO}$ is basic but $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ is amphoteric.
(1) B and D only
(2) C and D only
(3) B and C only
(4) A and E only
question.html:
Which of the following statements are INCORRECT? Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A) All the transition metals except scandium form MO oxides which are ionic.
  2. (B) The highest oxidation number corresponding to the group number in transition metal oxides is attained in Sc2O3 to Mn2O7.
  3. (C) Basic character increases from V2O3 to V2O4 to V2O5.
  4. (D) V2O4 dissolves in acids to give VO43- salts.
  5. (E) CrO is basic but Cr2O3 is amphoteric.
  1. (1)B and D only
  2. (2)C and D only
  3. (3)B and C only
  4. (4)A and E only
question.stem: Which of the following statements are INCORRECT? Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

statements.label: A
statements.text: All the transition metals except scandium form $\mathrm{MO}$ oxides which are ionic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The highest oxidation number corresponding to the group number in transition metal oxides is attained in $\mathrm{Sc_2O_3}$ to $\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}$.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Basic character increases from $\mathrm{V_2O_3}$ to $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ to $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$.

statements.label: D
statements.text: $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ dissolves in acids to give $\mathrm{VO_4^{3-}}$ salts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: $\mathrm{CrO}$ is basic but $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ is amphoteric.

steps: A: all transition metals except Sc form ionic $\mathrm{MO}$ oxides, so A is correct.
B: oxides from $\mathrm{Sc_2O_3}$ to $\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}$ show the highest oxidation state equal to the group number, so B is correct.
C: as oxidation state of V rises, $\mathrm{V_2O_3}$ (basic) $\to$ $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ (less basic) $\to$ $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$ (amphoteric), so basic character decreases and C is incorrect.
D: $\mathrm{V_2O_4}$ dissolves in acids to give $\mathrm{VO^{2+}}$ salts, not $\mathrm{VO_4^{3-}}$, so D is incorrect.
E: $\mathrm{CrO}$ is basic and $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ is amphoteric, so E is correct.
Incorrect statements are C and D, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A: all transition metals except Sc form ionic MO oxides, so A is correct.
  2. B: oxides from Sc2O3 to Mn2O7 show the highest oxidation state equal to the group number, so B is correct.
  3. C: as oxidation state of V rises, V2O3 (basic) → V2O4 (less basic) → V2O5 (amphoteric), so basic character decreases and C is incorrect.
  4. D: V2O4 dissolves in acids to give VO2+ salts, not VO43-, so D is incorrect.
  5. E: CrO is basic and Cr2O3 is amphoteric, so E is correct.
  6. Incorrect statements are C and D, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: C is wrong (basic character decreases V2O3 > V2O4 > V2O5) and D is wrong (V2O4 dissolves in acids to give VO2+ salts); A, B, E are correct as in NCERT.

question.full_text:
The reaction that does NOT take place in a blast furnace between $900\,\mathrm{K}$ to $1500\,\mathrm{K}$ temperature range during extraction of iron is :
(1) $\mathrm{FeO + CO \rightarrow Fe + CO_2}$
(2) $\mathrm{C + CO_2 \rightarrow 2CO}$
(3) $\mathrm{CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3}$
(4) $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + CO \rightarrow 2FeO + CO_2}$
question.html:
The reaction that does NOT take place in a blast furnace between 900 K to 1500 K temperature range during extraction of iron is :
  1. (1)FeO + CO → Fe + CO2
  2. (2)C + CO2 → 2CO
  3. (3)CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3
  4. (4)Fe2O3 + CO → 2FeO + CO2
question.stem: The reaction that does NOT take place in a blast furnace between $900\,\mathrm{K}$ to $1500\,\mathrm{K}$ temperature range during extraction of iron is :

steps: In the blast furnace, the $500$-$800\,\mathrm{K}$ zone has $\mathrm{3Fe_2O_3 + CO \rightarrow 2Fe_3O_4 + CO_2}$, $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4 + 4CO \rightarrow 3Fe + 4CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + CO \rightarrow 2FeO + CO_2}$.

The $900$-$1500\,\mathrm{K}$ zone has $\mathrm{C + CO_2 \rightarrow 2CO}$ and $\mathrm{FeO + CO \rightarrow Fe + CO_2}$; limestone decomposes and $\mathrm{CaO + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3}$ forms slag in the hotter region.
So $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + CO \rightarrow 2FeO + CO_2}$ does not take place at $900$-$1500\,\mathrm{K}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In the blast furnace, the 500-800 K zone has 3Fe2O3 + CO → 2Fe3O4 + CO2, Fe3O4 + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO2 and Fe2O3 + CO → 2FeO + CO2.
  2. The 900-1500 K zone has C + CO2 → 2CO and FeO + CO → Fe + CO2; limestone decomposes and CaO + SiO2 → CaSiO3 forms slag in the hotter region.
  3. So Fe2O3 + CO → 2FeO + CO2 does not take place at 900-1500 K, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Per NCERT, Fe2O3 + CO -> 2FeO + CO2 occurs in the lower-temperature zone (500-800 K); C + CO2 -> 2CO and FeO + CO -> Fe + CO2 occur at 900-1500 K, and slag formation (CaO + SiO2) occurs in the hotter region.

figures.text: i. naphthalene; ii. cyclopentadienide anion; iii. cyclobutadiene; iv. cyclopropenide anion; v. cyclopropenylium cation; vi. cyclooctatetraene; vii. anthracene

steps: i. Naphthalene: planar, cyclic, conjugated with $10\,\pi$ electrons $= 4(2)+2$, so it obeys Huckel's rule.
ii. Cyclopentadienyl anion: $4\,\pi$ electrons from two C=C plus the lone pair gives $6\,\pi$ electrons $= 4(1)+2$, so it obeys.
iii. Cyclobutadiene: $4\,\pi$ electrons $= 4n$ with $n=1$, antiaromatic, does not obey.
iv. Cyclopropenyl anion: $2\,\pi$ from C=C plus the lone pair gives $4\,\pi$ electrons $= 4n$, does not obey.
v. Cyclopropenyl cation: $2\,\pi$ electrons $= 4(0)+2$, so it obeys.
vi. Cyclooctatetraene: $8\,\pi$ electrons $= 4n$ and tub-shaped (non-planar), does not obey.
vii. Anthracene: $14\,\pi$ electrons $= 4(3)+2$, so it obeys.
Species obeying: i, ii, v, vii, so the count is $4$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. i. Naphthalene: planar, cyclic, conjugated with 10 π electrons = 4(2)+2, so it obeys Huckel's rule.
  2. ii. Cyclopentadienyl anion: 4 π electrons from two C=C plus the lone pair gives 6 π electrons = 4(1)+2, so it obeys.
  3. iii. Cyclobutadiene: 4 π electrons = 4n with n=1, antiaromatic, does not obey.
  4. iv. Cyclopropenyl anion: 2 π from C=C plus the lone pair gives 4 π electrons = 4n, does not obey.
  5. v. Cyclopropenyl cation: 2 π electrons = 4(0)+2, so it obeys.
  6. vi. Cyclooctatetraene: 8 π electrons = 4n and tub-shaped (non-planar), does not obey.
  7. vii. Anthracene: 14 π electrons = 4(3)+2, so it obeys.
  8. Species obeying: i, ii, v, vii, so the count is 4, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Naphthalene (10 pi), cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi), cyclopropenyl cation (2 pi) and anthracene (14 pi) obey 4n+2; cyclobutadiene, cyclopropenyl anion and cyclooctatetraene do not, so 4.

chapter.why: The answer depends on applying Huckel's (4n+2) pi-electron rule to decide which compounds/ions are aromatic, which is the Aromaticity topic of General Organic Chemistry.

subtopics.name: Aromaticity
subtopics.why: The answer depends on counting species that satisfy Huckel's (4n+2) pi-electron rule, which is the criterion for aromaticity.

step_list: For each of the seven species, check that it is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated (decide whether the charged carbon or lone pair joins the pi system, and whether the 8-membered ring stays planar)
Count the pi electrons in each, including the lone pair on the anions and the empty p orbital on the cation
Treat the fused polycycles (naphthalene, anthracene) by counting the whole periphery pi electrons (10 and 14)
Test each count against 4n+2, telling apart the 4-pi species (cyclobutadiene, cyclopropenyl anion, cyclooctatetraene with 8) from the 2/6/10/14-pi ones
Tally the species that pass and match the total to an option
difficulty.why: One rule (Huckel 4n+2 with the planarity/conjugation conditions) has to be applied independently to seven structures, each needing its own pi-electron count, and then tallied, so a single misjudgement changes the answer.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Paired near-identical traps: the cyclopropenyl anion and cation differ only in the sign of the charge (4 vs 2 pi electrons), and cyclooctatetraene looks like a conjugated ring but is non-planar with 8 pi electrons; miscounting one of these lands exactly on a neighbouring option (5 or 6).

source.note: Seven labelled structures (i.-vii.) between the first stem line and the question line are drawn in the figure; not transcribed here, left for figure transcriber. Options are plain numbers.

trap.feels: the two anions look alike on the page, both a ring with a negative charge and a lone pair drawn on one carbon, and one of them really is aromatic

steps.fix: Count the electrons: one double bond plus the lone pair is four, which is $4n$, not $4n+2$. On the three-membered ring it is the cation, with two pi electrons, that is aromatic.

other_options.feels: six of the seven species are closed conjugated rings, so counting all but the obviously antiaromatic cyclobutadiene looks thorough

Every other ring on the list is fully conjugated, so the tally is 6.
steps.fix: The rule asks for $4n+2$ electrons in a planar ring: the cyclopropenide anion holds four, and cyclooctatetraene holds eight and is tub-shaped, so neither counts.

other_options.feels: naphthalene and anthracene are the two species on the list that are visibly made of benzene rings, so 2 looks like the safe answer

steps.fix: Huckel's rule is about the electron count, not the ring size or the charge: the cyclopentadienide anion with six and the cyclopropenylium cation with two both satisfy it.

steps: Options $1$, $3$ and $4$ contain only monodentate ligands ($\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{Br^-}$).
Option $2$, $\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]NO_3}$, contains two bidentate $\mathrm{en}$ ligands that form chelate rings with $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$.

  2. Option 2, [CoCl2(en)2]NO3, contains two bidentate en ligands that form chelate rings with Co3+.
  3. Chelation (chelate effect) greatly increases complex stability, so option 2 is the most stable.
ai_solution.why: Only option 2 has the bidentate chelating ligand ethylenediamine; the chelate effect makes [CoCl2(en)2]NO3 the most stable complex.

On balancing the given redox reaction, $\mathrm{aCr_2O_7^{2-} + bSO_3^{2-}(aq) + cH^{+}(aq) \rightarrow 2aCr^{3+}(aq) + bSO_4^{2-}(aq) + \frac{c}{2}H_2O(l)}$ the coefficients a, b and c are found to be, respectively-
(1) 3, 8, 1
(2) 1, 8, 3
(3) 8, 1, 3
(4) 1, 3, 8
question.html:
On balancing the given redox reaction, aCr2O72- + bSO32-(aq) + cH+(aq) → 2aCr3+(aq) + bSO42-(aq) + c2H2O(l) the coefficients a, b and c are found to be, respectively-
  1. (1)3, 8, 1
  2. (2)1, 8, 3
  3. (3)8, 1, 3

question.stem: On balancing the given redox reaction, $\mathrm{aCr_2O_7^{2-} + bSO_3^{2-}(aq) + cH^{+}(aq) \rightarrow 2aCr^{3+}(aq) + bSO_4^{2-}(aq) + \frac{c}{2}H_2O(l)}$ the coefficients a, b and c are found to be, respectively-

steps: Oxidation states: Cr in $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ is $+6$, in $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ is $+3$; S in $\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}$ is $+4$, in $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is $+6$.
Electrons gained per $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$: $2 \times 3 = 6$; electrons lost per $\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}$: $2$.
Equate electrons: $6a = 2b \Rightarrow b = 3a$; take $a = 1$, $b = 3$.
Charge balance: left $-2 - 6 + c$, right $2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0$, so $c - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow c = 8$.
Check oxygen: left $7 + 9 = 16$, right $12 + \frac{c}{2} = 12 + 4 = 16$. Balanced.
$a, b, c = 1, 3, 8$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Oxidation states: Cr in Cr2O72- is +6, in Cr3+ is +3; S in SO32- is +4, in SO42- is +6.
  2. Electrons gained per Cr2O72-: 2 × 3 = 6; electrons lost per SO32-: 2.
  3. Equate electrons: 6a = 2b ⇒ b = 3a; take a = 1, b = 3.
  4. Charge balance: left -2 - 6 + c, right 2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0, so c - 8 = 0 ⇒ c = 8.
  5. Check oxygen: left 7 + 9 = 16, right 12 + c2 = 12 + 4 = 16. Balanced.
  6. a, b, c = 1, 3, 8, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: Cr goes +6 to +3 (gains 6 e- per Cr2O7^2-), S goes +4 to +6 (loses 2 e- per SO3^2-), so 1 dichromate : 3 sulfite; charge balance needs 8 H+, giving 4 H2O = c/2.

1. Peroxodisulphuric acid H2S2O8: HO-S(O2)-O-O-S(O2)-OH has two S-OH, four S=O and one S-O-O-S, so A → III.
  2. Sulphuric acid H2SO4: (HO)2S(=O)2 has two S-OH and two S=O, so B → IV.
  3. Pyrosulphuric acid H2S2O7: HO-S(O2)-O-S(O2)-OH has two S-OH, four S=O and one S-O-S, so C → I.
  4. Sulphurous acid H2SO3: (HO)2S=O has two S-OH and one S=O, so D → II.
  5. A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II is option 1.
ai_solution.why: H2S2O8 has an S-O-O-S peroxo link (III), H2SO4 has two S-OH and two S=O (IV), H2S2O7 has an S-O-S bridge (I), H2SO3 has two S-OH and one S=O (II).

trap.route: Nothing in the name "pyrosulphuric" announces two sulphur atoms the way "peroxodisulphuric" does, so read as a one-sulphur acid it cannot carry "Four S=O" and takes the one-S=O entry instead. steps.text: "Peroxo" names the O-O linkage, so peroxodisulphuric acid takes "One S-O-O-S", and sulphuric acid takes two S-OH with two S=O.
"Pyrosulphuric" names one sulphur, as sulphuric acid does, so four S=O is too many for it and it takes "Two S-OH, One S=O".
steps.fix: Pyro- means two acid units condensed with the loss of water: pyrosulphuric acid is $\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}$, two sulphurs carrying two S=O each.

steps.text: The bridged entry is then left for sulphurous acid.
steps.fix: $\mathrm{H_2SO_3}$ has a single sulphur, so an S-O-S bridge has nothing to bridge; one sulphur holding two OH leaves exactly one S=O.

other_options.who: a student who can draw sulphurous acid as $\mathrm{(HO)_2S{=}O}$ and reads "disulphuric" in the first name as the whole of the bridge story, without stopping on "peroxo"
other_options.feels: Both bridged entries print "Two S-OH, Four S=O", so one oxygen in the bridge is all that separates them, and "One S-O-S" is the simpler bridge to hand to the name that ends in "disulphuric"

steps.text: Sulphurous acid is $\mathrm{(HO)_2S{=}O}$, so D takes "Two S-OH, One S=O".
Peroxodisulphuric acid is the two-sulphur acid with a bridge, so it takes "One S-O-S".
steps.fix: Count the oxygens in the bridge: "peroxo" is the O-O linkage, so this acid takes "One S-O-O-S" and the plain S-O-S bridge belongs to pyrosulphuric acid.

steps.text: The peroxide entry is then left for sulphuric acid.
steps.fix: $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ holds one sulphur and no bridge at all, so an entry carrying "One S-O-O-S" cannot be its bond set.

steps: A: detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles (fragmentation), so A is true.
B: humus is degraded very slowly by some microbes and releases inorganic nutrients by mineralization, so B is true.
C: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts by leaching, so C is true.
D: the detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter (detritus), not living organisms, so D is false.
E: earthworms breaking detritus into smaller particles is fragmentation; catabolism is enzymatic degradation by bacteria and fungi, so E is false.
True set is $\{A, B, C\}$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A: detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles (fragmentation), so A is true.
  2. B: humus is degraded very slowly by some microbes and releases inorganic nutrients by mineralization, so B is true.
  3. C: water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts by leaching, so C is true.
  4. D: the detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter (detritus), not living organisms, so D is false.
  5. E: earthworms breaking detritus into smaller particles is fragmentation; catabolism is enzymatic degradation by bacteria and fungi, so E is false.
  6. True set is {A, B, C}, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: A, B, C are true (fragmentation by detritivores, humus mineralised by microbes, leaching); D false (detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter) and E false (that is fragmentation, not catabolism).

question.stem: In angiosperm, the haploid, diploid and triploid structures of a fertilized embryo sac sequentially are :

answer.publisher_text: Synergids, Zygote and Primary endosperm nucleus
answer.ai_text: Synergids, Zygote and Primary endosperm nucleus

steps: Synergids are cells of the egg apparatus, formed from the haploid megaspore, so they are haploid ($n$).
Syngamy fuses the egg ($n$) with one male gamete ($n$): zygote $= n + n = 2n$ (diploid).
Triple fusion joins two polar nuclei ($n + n$) with the second male gamete ($n$): PEN $= 3n$ (triploid).
The order haploid, diploid, triploid is synergids, zygote, primary endosperm nucleus, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Synergids are cells of the egg apparatus, formed from the haploid megaspore, so they are haploid (n).
  2. Syngamy fuses the egg (n) with one male gamete (n): zygote = n + n = 2n (diploid).
  3. Triple fusion joins two polar nuclei (n + n) with the second male gamete (n): PEN = 3n (triploid).
  4. The order haploid, diploid, triploid is synergids, zygote, primary endosperm nucleus, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Synergids are haploid (n), the zygote is diploid (2n) and the primary endosperm nucleus is triploid (3n), in that order.

steps: M phase (mitosis) is the equational division, so A-IV.
In $\mathrm{G_2}$ phase proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, so B-I.

  2. In G2 phase proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, so B-I.
  3. The quiescent stage (G0) is an inactive phase, so C-II.
  4. G1 phase is the interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication, so D-III.
  5. A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III matches option 2.
ai_solution.why: M phase is equational division, proteins are synthesised in G2, the quiescent stage (G0) is inactive, and G1 is the interval between mitosis and the start of DNA replication.

categories.concept: Each phase of the cell cycle has its own job: G1 is the gap before DNA replication, G2 is where proteins are made for mitosis, M is the equational division, and G0 is the inactive stage cells park in

trap.label: wrong_site_attacked

steps.text: M phase is the equational division, and G1 is the interval between mitosis and the initiation of DNA replication.
G2 is a gap, so G2 is the inactive phase, and protein synthesis must belong to the quiescent stage.
steps.fix: The inactive stage is G0, the quiescent stage that cells enter when they stop dividing; G2 is the phase in which proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis.

Checked row by row: it pairs M Phase with 'Interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication', a description that places the phase after mitosis and so cannot be mitosis, and it puts 'Equational division' on the quiescent stage, which is defined by cells having stopped dividing. Two rows would have to contradict their own wording at once.

steps: Mutualism benefits both species: $+(A), +(B)$, so $A \rightarrow IV$.
Commensalism benefits one species and leaves the other unaffected: $+(A), 0(B)$, so $B \rightarrow I$.
Amensalism harms one species and leaves the other unaffected: $-(A), 0(B)$, so $C \rightarrow II$.
Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host: $+(A), -(B)$, so $D \rightarrow III$.
$A$-IV, $B$-I, $C$-II, $D$-III matches option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Mutualism benefits both species: +(A), +(B), so A → IV.
  2. Commensalism benefits one species and leaves the other unaffected: +(A), 0(B), so B → I.
  3. Amensalism harms one species and leaves the other unaffected: -(A), 0(B), so C → II.
  4. Parasitism benefits the parasite and harms the host: +(A), -(B), so D → III.
  5. A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III matches option 1.
ai_solution.why: Mutualism +/+ (IV), commensalism +/0 (I), amensalism -/0 (II), parasitism +/- (III): A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

  4. D: bark includes the periderm and the secondary phloem, so D is true.
  5. E: phellogen is a couple of layers thick, not single-layered, so E is false.
  6. True statements are A and D only, which is option 1.

question.full_text:
Match List I with List II. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
List-I: (A) A Leopard and a Lion in a forest/grassland; (B) A Cuckoo laying egg in a Crow’s nest; (C) Fungi and root of a higher plant in Mycorrhizae; (D) A cattle egret and a Cattle in a field
List-II: (I) Competition; (II) Brood parasitism; (III) Mutualism; (IV) Commensalism
(1) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
(2) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
(3) A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
(4) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
question.html:
Match List I with List II. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
List-IList-II
AA Leopard and a Lion in a forest/grasslandICompetition
BA Cuckoo laying egg in a Crow’s nestIIBrood parasitism
CFungi and root of a higher plant in MycorrhizaeIIIMutualism
DA cattle egret and a Cattle in a fieldIVCommensalism
  1. (1)A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
  2. (2)A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
  3. (3)A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
  4. (4)A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
question.stem: Match List I with List II. Choose the correct answer from the options given below.

list_i.label: A
list_i.text: A Leopard and a Lion in a forest/grassland

list_i.label: B
list_i.text: A Cuckoo laying egg in a Crow’s nest

list_i.label: C

list_i.label: D

steps: A leopard and a lion share prey in the same habitat, so A is competition: $A \to I$.
A cuckoo lays its eggs in a crow's nest for the host to incubate, so B is brood parasitism: $B \to II$.
In mycorrhizae the fungus and the plant root both benefit, so C is mutualism: $C \to III$.
The cattle egret feeds on insects stirred up by grazing cattle and the cattle are unaffected, so D is commensalism: $D \to IV$.
$A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV$ matches option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A leopard and a lion share prey in the same habitat, so A is competition: A → I.
  2. A cuckoo lays its eggs in a crow's nest for the host to incubate, so B is brood parasitism: B → II.
  3. In mycorrhizae the fungus and the plant root both benefit, so C is mutualism: C → III.
  4. The cattle egret feeds on insects stirred up by grazing cattle and the cattle are unaffected, so D is commensalism: D → IV.
  5. A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV matches option 4.
ai_solution.why: Leopard-lion compete (I), cuckoo is a brood parasite (II), mycorrhiza is mutualism (III), cattle egret-cattle is commensalism (IV).

categories.concept: Interactions are named from who gains and who loses: two big cats after the same prey compete, a cuckoo in a crow's nest is a brood parasite, fungus and root in a mycorrhiza both gain, and the egret gains while the cattle are unaffected

trap.label: nearby_fact
trap.route: The cattle egret is moved one box over into mutualism by crediting the cattle with a benefit from the insects the egret takes, and commensalism is then the only label left for the mycorrhiza
trap.who: a student who knows the egret follows grazing cattle and reasons out the exchange instead of recalling the box the chapter prints the example in
trap.feels: the code keeps competition and brood parasitism, the two rows whose examples name themselves, so only the two rows about benefit move and the egret story sounds like an exchange of favours

steps.text: Two big cats hunting the same prey compete, and a cuckoo laying in a crow's nest is a brood parasite.
The egret eats the insects the cattle stir up and clears pests off them, so both gain — mutualism — and the mycorrhiza is left as commensalism.
steps.fix: The cattle egret and the grazing cattle are the chapter's example of commensalism: the egret gains and the cattle are neither helped nor harmed. In a mycorrhiza both the fungus and the root gain, which is mutualism.

other_options.proof: Checked the rows that fix this code: a leopard and a lion as mutualism and the mycorrhiza as competition. Mutualism requires both partners to gain, and nothing in 'A Leopard and a Lion in a forest/grassland' supplies a gain for either; competition requires a shared resource, and a fungus living in a root supplies none. Both rows contradict the printed example.

Checked the rows that fix this code: the leopard and lion as brood parasitism and the cuckoo and crow as mutualism. Brood parasitism is defined by an egg laid in another bird's nest, which only row B supplies, and the cuckoo's egg costs the crow its own brood, so neither row can carry the label this code gives it.

categories.reason: This question requires the interaction each printed example illustrates, demonstrated by row D, 'A cattle egret and a Cattle in a field', set against 'Commensalism'.
categories.note: nearby_fact rather than look_alike_term: mutualism and commensalism do not resemble each other as words, and the pull is that they are adjacent boxes in the same list of interactions with the egret printed under one of them — rename the categories and the pull survives, so position is doing the work. The key here is also the straight positional code A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV, so no option can be struck out for being the parallel mapping.

question.full_text:
Vital capacity of lung is _________.
(1) $\mathrm{IRV + ERV + TV + RV}$
(2) $\mathrm{IRV + ERV + TV - RV}$
(3) $\mathrm{IRV + ERV + TV}$
(4) $\mathrm{IRV + ERV}$
question.html:
Vital capacity of lung is _________.
  1. (1)IRV + ERV + TV + RV
  2. (2)IRV + ERV + TV - RV
  3. (3)IRV + ERV + TV
  4. (4)IRV + ERV
question.stem: Vital capacity of lung is _________.

steps: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration, so $VC = \mathrm{IRV + TV + ERV}$, which excludes $\mathrm{RV}$; this is option $3$.
ai_solution.html: 1. Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration, so VC = IRV + TV + ERV, which excludes RV; this is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Vital capacity is the maximum air breathed out after a forced inspiration: ERV + TV + IRV (RV is not included).

chapter.name: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
chapter.why: The answer depends on the definition of vital capacity as IRV + ERV + TV, a respiratory capacity taught in Breathing and Exchange of Gases.

subtopics.name: Respiratory Volumes and Capacities
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the definition of vital capacity as IRV + ERV + TV, which is taught under respiratory volumes and capacities.

step_list: Recall the NCERT definition of vital capacity as the maximum volume exhaled after a forced inspiration, expressed as the sum of the component lung volumes, and match it to the option
difficulty.why: The work is a single recall of the NCERT formula for vital capacity in terms of tidal, inspiratory reserve and expiratory reserve volumes.

source.note: Options are sums of lung volume abbreviations, written as LaTeX expressions; the en dash in option 2 is written as a minus sign.

categories.concept: Vital capacity is all the air a person can actually move - IRV plus TV plus ERV - and it leaves out the residual volume, which cannot be breathed out

trap.label: answers_other_question
trap.route: This is the printed sum for total lung capacity, which the same section defines as RV, ERV, TV and IRV together, so a student who has learnt one four-term sum for the lungs writes it here; vital capacity is the same sum with the residual volume taken out, because that volume can never be exhaled
trap.who: a student who has learnt the capacities as sums of the four volumes and has not kept which sum belongs to which capacity
trap.feels: it is the most complete expression on the page and it is a genuine printed capacity, so it reads as the fuller and therefore the better answer

steps.text: The capacities are built by adding up the respiratory volumes, and this is one of the printed sums.
So vital capacity is all four volumes added together.
steps.fix: All four together is total lung capacity; vital capacity is measured by breathing, so the residual volume, which stays in the lungs, is excluded.

other_options.who: a student who has stored the shortcut that vital capacity is total lung capacity minus the residual volume and then expands the total wrongly
other_options.feels: the expression visibly subtracts the residual volume, which is exactly the correction the student knows is needed

steps.text: Vital capacity is the total lung capacity with the residual volume removed.
So it is IRV + ERV + TV - RV.
steps.fix: IRV + ERV + TV is already the total with RV removed; subtracting RV a second time takes out a volume that was never in the sum.

other_options.who: a student who reads vital capacity as the extra air available beyond ordinary breathing
other_options.feels: the two reserve volumes are the ones a forced breath calls on, so the capacity measured by a forced breath looks like just those two

steps.text: A forced inspiration and a forced expiration bring in the two reserve volumes.
So vital capacity is IRV + ERV.
steps.fix: The forced breath also moves the tidal volume, so TV is part of vital capacity; only RV is left out.

categories.reason: This question requires one printed definition, demonstrated by the blank in 'Vital capacity of lung is _________.' with four rival sums of the respiratory volumes as options.
categories.note: E1 returned fill_in_blank, which the codebook treats as an overlay rather than a shape; the primary printed shape is a plain four-answer question, so qtype is recorded as mcq.

question.stem: Math List I with List II. Choose the correct answer from the options given below :

steps: CCK acts on the pancreas (pancreatic enzyme secretion) and gall bladder, so $A \to IV$.
GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility, so it relates to the gastric gland: $B \to III$.
ANF is secreted by the atrial wall of the heart: $C \to II$.
ADH acts on the distal tubules of the kidney: $D \to I$.
$A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I$ is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility, so it relates to the gastric gland: B → III.
  3. ANF is secreted by the atrial wall of the heart: C → II.
  4. ADH acts on the distal tubules of the kidney: D → I.
  5. A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I is option 4.
ai_solution.why: CCK acts on pancreas (and gall bladder), GIP inhibits gastric gland secretion, ANF is secreted by the heart, ADH acts on the kidney: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

steps: A: tetrads are seen in pachytene after synapsis in zygotene, not leptotene, so A is false.
B: in (mitotic) anaphase the centromeres split and sister chromatids separate, so B is true.
C: terminalisation of chiasmata occurs in diakinesis, not pachytene, so C is false.
D: in telophase the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform, so D is true.
E: crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, so E is false.
True statements are B and D only, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A: tetrads are seen in pachytene after synapsis in zygotene, not leptotene, so A is false.
  2. B: in (mitotic) anaphase the centromeres split and sister chromatids separate, so B is true.
  3. C: terminalisation of chiasmata occurs in diakinesis, not pachytene, so C is false.
  4. D: in telophase the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform, so D is true.
  5. E: crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, so E is false.
  6. True statements are B and D only, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: A false (tetrads/bivalents form in zygotene-pachytene), C false (terminalisation in diakinesis), E false (crossing over is between non-sister chromatids); B and D true.

(1) B, C and D only
(2) A, B and E only
(3) C, D and E only
(4) A and B only

  1. (A) An excessive loss of body fluid from the body switches off osmoreceptors.
  2. (B) ADH facilitates water reabsorption to prevent diuresis.
  3. (C) ANF causes vasodilation.
  4. (D) ADH causes increase in blood pressure.
  5. (E) ADH is responsible for decrease in GFR.

steps: A: excessive loss of body fluid activates osmoreceptors, which trigger ADH release, so A is false.
B: ADH facilitates water reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct, preventing diuresis, so B is true.
C: ANF causes vasodilation and lowers blood pressure, so C is true.
D: ADH constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure, so D is true.
E: by raising blood pressure, ADH can increase glomerular blood flow and GFR, not decrease it, so E is false.
True set $= \{B, C, D\}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A: excessive loss of body fluid activates osmoreceptors, which trigger ADH release, so A is false.
  2. B: ADH facilitates water reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct, preventing diuresis, so B is true.
  3. C: ANF causes vasodilation and lowers blood pressure, so C is true.
  4. D: ADH constricts blood vessels, raising blood pressure, so D is true.
  5. E: by raising blood pressure, ADH can increase glomerular blood flow and GFR, not decrease it, so E is false.
  6. True set = {B, C, D}, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: A is false (fluid loss activates, not switches off, osmoreceptors); B, C, D are true; E is false (ADH raises BP and so can increase GFR), giving B, C and D only.

question.full_text:
Which one of the following is NOT an advantage of inbreeding?
(1) It exposes harmful recessive genes but are eliminated by selection.
(2) Elimination of less desirable genes and accumulation of superior genes takes place due to it.
(3) It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.
(4) It decreases homozygosity.
question.html:
Which one of the following is NOT an advantage of inbreeding?
  1. (1)It exposes harmful recessive genes but are eliminated by selection.
  2. (2)Elimination of less desirable genes and accumulation of superior genes takes place due to it.
  3. (3)It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.
  4. (4)It decreases homozygosity.
question.stem: Which one of the following is NOT an advantage of inbreeding?

options.text: It exposes harmful recessive genes but are eliminated by selection.
Elimination of less desirable genes and accumulation of superior genes takes place due to it.
It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.

answer.publisher_text: It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.
answer.ai_text: It decreases the productivity of inbred population, after continuous inbreeding.

steps: Inbreeding is mating of closely related individuals for $4$-$6$ generations, so it $\textit{increases}$ homozygosity.
Exposing harmful recessive genes so selection removes them (option $1$) is an advantage.
Eliminating less desirable genes and accumulating superior genes (option $2$) is an advantage.
Continued inbreeding reduces fertility and productivity, i.e. inbreeding depression (option $3$), which is a disadvantage.
Option $4$ is factually false (inbreeding increases homozygosity), so it is also not an advantage; the intended disadvantage is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Inbreeding is mating of closely related individuals for 4-6 generations, so it increases homozygosity.
  2. Exposing harmful recessive genes so selection removes them (option 1) is an advantage.
  3. Eliminating less desirable genes and accumulating superior genes (option 2) is an advantage.
  4. Continued inbreeding reduces fertility and productivity, i.e. inbreeding depression (option 3), which is a disadvantage.
  5. Option 4 is factually false (inbreeding increases homozygosity), so it is also not an advantage; the intended disadvantage is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Continuous inbreeding reduces fertility and productivity (inbreeding depression), which is a disadvantage, not an advantage; options 1 and 2 are NCERT-listed advantages.

question.stem: Which one of the following is the sequence on corresponding coding strand, if the sequence on mRNA formed is as follows 5’AUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCGAUCG AUCG 3’?

steps: The coding strand has the same sequence and the same $5' \rightarrow 3'$ polarity as the mRNA, except that DNA has $T$ where RNA has $U$.

ai_solution.html:
1. The coding strand has the same sequence and the same 5' → 3' polarity as the mRNA, except that DNA has T where RNA has U.
  2. Replacing U with T in 5' AUCG… AUCG 3' gives 5' ATCG… ATCG 3', which is option 2.
